Please don't hurt me, some of what I'm about to say goes against the grain of most Next Gen sentiment I come across

  1. Rose and Scorpius don't ever pursue a romantic relationship. Ever. They might be friends, they might not be. I could see them having a healthy rivalry in the Ministry after Hogwarts.

  7. James Sirius finds a way to exorcise Binns.

This is the wrong way to think of it. What you're asking is akin to asking what is the best wire to buy if I want to wire a house for electricity but I'm not an electrician. There is so much more to being a programmer than knowing syntax that saying I want to learn a language is well intentioned but wrong.

The language really doesn't matter -- well it does, but let's keep it simple at this point -- what does matter is developing the mind set that goes along with programming. It's the way to solve problems using a tool, or set of tools, under very well defined but complex constraints.

The best programmers I've ever met are all self-taught. They had the will and curiosity to figure things out on their own, and the self awareness to know when too ask for help. Some started with machine code, some with assembler, some with BASIC, some with Pascal, some with C... I hope you get my point here.

So don't think of it as which language. Rather think of it as I want to solve a problem, which tools are well suited and how do I start, and then go from there.

If you just want to learn a language but don't actually have a project in mind then you probably won't learn a language. At least that's how I see it.

[edit] If you're at a loss for a project then you could try doing The Towers of Hanoi, which is a popular beginner programmer assignment. Or read up on the various sorting algorithms and attempt to implement one of those. Either of these are easy enough that you won't get hung up on the problem itself, yet complex enough that you'll have to devise a multi-step solution.

In any case, whatever language you learn, you should stick to one at first and get it down well. If you know one language deeply, you'll see the similarities in other languages and be able to lean on what you already know. Don't stress too much about which one to start with, and just start with one.
